passage: At the Sunday meeting of the Velachery residents' association, Hemant, the secretary, stood up with a printout. "Before anything else: Varun organised the lake-edge clean-up last week. Sixty volunteers, forty bags of rubbish, and he got the corporation truck to come on a Sunday. Thank you, Varun." People clapped. Varun's ears went red. "Arre, it was nothing, anyone could have done it," he said, waving a hand. Hemant's smile flickered; he lowered the printout a little, as if he'd said something wrong. Varun saw it. He'd done this all his life, batting praise away, and he suddenly realised it made the other person feel foolish for offering it. He stood up. "Actually, thank you, Hemant. I'm proud of it. And the real credit goes to the Class 9 kids from the school, who worked four hours straight." The kids at the back cheered. Hemant grinned and sat down.

qa.q: How many bags of rubbish were collected?
qa.a: Forty bags of rubbish.

qa.q: How did Hemant seem to feel when Varun said 'it was nothing'?
qa.a: Hemant seemed deflated and a little foolish, his smile flickering and the printout lowering, as if his thanks had been a mistake.

qa.q: How did Varun receive the praise the second time?
qa.a: He thanked Hemant simply, admitted being proud, and credited the Class 9 kids, balancing acceptance with credit to others.

qa.q: How might the Class 9 kids have felt when Varun credited them?
qa.a: They were delighted and proud, cheering from the back at being publicly recognised for four hours of work.

grounding: Shows a young adult brushing off public thanks, noticing it leaves the giver unheard, and then accepting warmly while crediting others.

passage:
"Farida, can I say something? Thank you for covering the client call on Friday. You saved me."
Farida didn't look up from her screen. "Oh, please. It was nothing. Anyone would have done it."
"It wasn't nothing. You stayed till eight."
"I had to stay anyway. Honestly, don't mention it."
Devika stood there a moment. "Okay," she said quietly, and turned to go.
Farida heard the flatness in it and looked up. "Wait. Sorry. I do that. My mother taught us to wave compliments away." She took a breath. "Thank you for saying it. I'm glad it helped, and I'm glad you noticed."
Devika's face relaxed. "I did. The client emailed to say the call was the clearest they'd had."
"Really?" Farida smiled. "Then Raghav deserves some of that. He built the slides."
"I'll tell him too."
"Tell him first."

qa.q: Until what time did Farida stay on Friday?
qa.a: Till eight.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Farida kept brushing off the thanks?
qa.a: Devika felt unheard and a bit hurt, her 'Okay' going flat as she turned to leave.

qa.q: What did Farida do to receive the thanks well?
qa.a: She apologised for brushing it off, thanked Devika, said she was glad it helped, and credited Raghav for the slides.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel when he hears about the client's email?
qa.a: Raghav would likely feel pleased and valued, since his slides were credited for the clearest call the client had had.

grounding: Shows a young professional deflecting thanks until she notices the giver feels unheard, then accepting warmly and crediting a colleague.

passage: When I won the young achiever award at our NGO last year, I gave a speech I still cringe at. I talked for four minutes about the literacy project: my idea, my late nights, my plan. I didn't mention Amandeep once, and she had run every single Saturday session at the settlement school with me. I saw her clapping politely at the back, not quite smiling. Afterwards she said lightly, "Nice speech, Alka," and went home early. It took me two days to understand. I had swung from the modest girl who used to say "it was nothing" to someone who took all the credit. So I called her. "I left you out. That was wrong. The project is half yours." She was quiet, then said, "Thank you for saying that." This year, when our director thanked me in the staff meeting, I said, "Thank you. I'm proud of it. Amandeep and I built it together." She squeezed my arm.

qa.q: What did Amandeep run with Alka?
qa.a: Every Saturday session at the settlement school.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt during Alka's award speech?
qa.a: Amandeep likely felt hurt and overlooked, clapping politely without really smiling and going home early.

qa.q: How did Alka balance recognition the second time?
qa.a: She said a simple thank-you, admitted pride, and credited Amandeep as co-builder, neither deflecting nor taking all the credit.

qa.q: What would have changed if Alka had never called Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep's hurt might have hardened into distrust, and their partnership on the project could have weakened.

grounding: A young adult recalls taking all the credit in an award speech, repairing it, and later accepting thanks warmly while crediting a partner.

passage: Bhupen, you thanked "the team" in your email today. Let me, Vasudha, tell you why I stopped doing that. At twenty-five I was leading my first project at the water-supply board in Guwahati. Our junior, Mridul, spotted that the pipe route crossed a flood zone and redrew it overnight. In the review with the chief engineer, I said, "We revised the route," and the chief praised me. Mridul sat very still. Later I heard he'd told a friend he felt invisible. I hadn't meant to steal it, but I had. So the next week, in front of the same chief, I said, "I want to correct something. The flood-zone catch was Mridul's. He redrew the route overnight. That probably saved us months." Mridul went red and grinned. He worked with me for ten more years. Name the person, Bhupen. Name what they did. Say it where the boss can hear.

qa.q: What did Mridul spot about the pipe route?
qa.a: That it crossed a flood zone.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when Vasudha said 'We revised the route'?
qa.a: Mridul felt invisible and hurt, sitting very still while Vasudha was praised for his catch.

qa.q: What choice repaired the situation?
qa.a: Correcting it the next week in front of the same chief, naming Mridul, exactly what he did and why it mattered.

qa.q: How might the chief engineer have seen the correction?
qa.a: The chief likely respected Vasudha more for giving honest credit, and learned who had actually caught the flood risk.

grounding: An elder recalls taking shared credit by accident and learning to give specific, timely, public credit to a teammate.

passage: The payment site had crashed at 11 pm on the biggest sale night of the year, and by 1 am it was back, thanks mostly to Hemant, who had traced the fault to a single expired certificate. The next morning Akash, the team lead, had exactly two minutes at the company all-hands before the chief executive's update. Two minutes, forty people on the call, and he hadn't slept. The easy thing was "Thanks to the team for last night." He'd heard that line a hundred times; it meant nothing. So he said, "Quick update: the outage lasted two hours. It was fixed because Hemant stayed calm, found an expired certificate in a file nobody had opened in a year, and walked the rest of us through the fix. Hemant, thank you. That saved the sale." In the chat, a dozen clapping hands appeared under Hemant's name. Hemant messaged Akash privately: "Nobody has ever said my name on that call before."

qa.q: What fault did Hemant find?
qa.a: An expired certificate in a file nobody had opened in a year.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Akash named him on the call?
qa.a: Hemant felt seen and moved, messaging that nobody had ever said his name on that call before.

qa.q: What made Akash's credit effective despite the time pressure?
qa.a: It was timely, public and specific: he named Hemant, what he found and how it saved the sale, instead of a generic thanks to the team.

qa.q: What would have changed if Akash had only said 'Thanks to the team'?
qa.a: Hemant's work would have stayed invisible, and the thanks would have meant as little as it always had.

grounding: Shows a young team lead giving specific, timely, public credit to a colleague under time pressure instead of generic praise.

passage: Lokesh still remembered the sting from his first job in Hyderabad: a manager presenting his research as "our findings" without a glance in his direction. So when Zainab, the new analyst on his team, spent her weekend cleaning up the messy survey data, he didn't wait. On Monday at ten, before the client report went out, he posted in the team group: "Before this goes to the client: Zainab rebuilt the survey dataset over the weekend and caught 312 duplicate responses. Without that, our main finding would have been wrong. Thank you, Zainab." He copied their director, Mrs. Rao. Zainab replied with a small 🙏 and nothing else. But at lunch she came over. "In my last job, nobody ever named who did what," she said. "I didn't know it could feel like this." Mrs. Rao asked Zainab to present the data section to the client that Friday.

qa.q: How many duplicate responses did Zainab catch?
qa.a: 312 duplicate responses.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she spoke to Lokesh at lunch?
qa.a: Zainab felt appreciated and moved, surprised by how good it felt to be named for her work, unlike in her last job.

qa.q: What made Lokesh's credit strong?
qa.a: It was timely, before the report went out, public in the team group with the director copied, and specific about what Zainab did and why it mattered.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Rao respond to the message?
qa.a: Mrs. Rao took notice and asked Zainab to present the data section to the client that Friday.

grounding: Shows a young professional crediting a teammate's specific contribution publicly and promptly, building trust.

passage: Kashish, you asked what helped when Appa died. Honestly? Not the messages. I got maybe eighty in the first day. Hearts, folded hands, "RIP uncle", "thinking of you". I knew people meant well. But after the twentieth heart I felt strangely lonelier, like everyone was waving from very far away. Then Nikhil called. He didn't say much. He asked, "Do you want me to come, or shall I just stay on the phone?" I said come. He sat on the floor of our hall with me for three hours while relatives came and went. He made tea. He answered the door. I don't remember a single message from that day, but I remember his socks, because one had a hole in the toe. So now, when something serious happens to someone, I still send the message. And then I ask if they'd like a call. That's what Appa's death taught me, Harsha, the one who used to only send hearts.

qa.q: How many messages did Harsha get on the first day?
qa.a: Maybe eighty messages.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel after the twentieth heart?
qa.a: Harsha felt strangely lonelier, as if everyone was waving from far away, despite knowing people meant well.

qa.q: What does Harsha now do when something serious happens to someone?
qa.a: Still sends a message, then asks whether they'd like a call, offering fuller presence if it is welcome.

qa.q: What might Nikhil's visit have meant for the household that day?
qa.a: It likely eased the day for the family too, since Nikhil made tea and answered the door while relatives came and went.

grounding: A young adult describes quick digital comfort feeling thin during grief, and a welcomed call and visit conveying care more fully.

passage: I'm Salma. When the news came into our team group that Ritu's house had flooded and her family was in a relief camp, the messages started at once: hearts, hugs, praying hands. Sharmila, sitting across from me, added a heart too, then stared at her phone for a long time. I couldn't tell what she was thinking. Maybe that the hearts felt thin next to a flooded house? She put the phone down, picked it up again and stepped out onto the balcony. Through the glass I watched her make a call, nodding a lot, talking slowly. When she came back she said, "Ritu picked up. She says the messages are sweet, but she's been sitting in the camp alone all afternoon. I'm going there after work with some dry clothes and a phone charger. Want to come?" I went. Ritu cried when she saw us, and then laughed at the size of the clothes.

qa.q: Where was Ritu's family staying?
qa.a: In a relief camp.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling as she stared at her phone?
qa.a: Sharmila may have felt uneasy that a heart seemed too thin for such a crisis, though Salma couldn't be sure what she was thinking.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do beyond the heart emoji, and why did it help?
qa.a: She called Ritu, learned she had been alone all afternoon, and visited with dry clothes and a charger, giving fuller care that Ritu welcomed.

qa.q: How did Ritu react when they arrived?
qa.a: Ritu cried with relief at seeing them and then laughed at the size of the clothes, clearly comforted by their presence.

grounding: An observer describes a heart emoji feeling thin during a colleague's crisis and a call and welcomed visit conveying fuller care.

passage:
Tuesday: Asif posted a short line in the friends' group: his Dadi had died that morning. Avni typed a heart and "So sorry, thinking of you," like everyone else. It felt too small, but she didn't know what else to do.
Thursday: Asif hadn't replied to anyone. Avni kept opening the chat and closing it. A heart felt like tapping on a window. But turning up at his door uninvited felt like too much.
Saturday: She called instead. He answered on the fourth ring, voice hoarse. "Hey. I didn't want to push," she said. "Would a visit help, or would you rather keep it to messages for now?" A long pause. "Honestly, not a visit yet. The house is full of relatives. But this call is nice." So they talked for twenty minutes about his Dadi's terrible jokes. Before hanging up he said, "Come on Wednesday, when it's quieter." She wrote it in her diary.

qa.q: When did Asif's Dadi die?
qa.a: On Tuesday morning.

qa.q: How did Avni feel on Thursday about the heart she had sent?
qa.a: Avni felt uneasy and helpless, sensing the heart was like tapping on a window, yet worried that turning up uninvited would be too much.

qa.q: What did Avni do that respected Asif's wishes?
qa.a: She called and asked whether he'd like a visit or messages, accepted 'not yet', kept him company on the phone, and planned the visit he suggested for Wednesday.

qa.q: What did the call mean for Asif?
qa.a: Asif found the call comforting even though he wasn't ready for a visit, sharing memories of his Dadi's jokes and inviting Avni for a quieter day.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from a heart emoji to a call during a friend's grief, and offering a visit only when it is welcome.

passage:
Wednesday night
Tarun called again at ten, second time this week, about his manager. Forty minutes. I listened, and afterwards I couldn't sleep, replaying his manager's words as if they'd been said to me. I've been carrying his week around like it's mine.
Today I tried something different. At lunch I listened properly for twenty minutes, and when I said, "It sounds like you felt humiliated in that meeting," he shook his head. "Not humiliated. Scared. I think I'm going to lose the job." I'd been guessing wrong all week.
Then I said the thing I'd practised. "I care about this, and I'm glad you tell me. But I'm not enough on my own. The company's counselling line is free and confidential; would you try it? And maybe we keep our chats to lunch, not late at night." He was quiet, then nodded. He booked a session while I was still eating.
Slept well tonight.
Kavitha

qa.q: How long was Tarun's call at ten?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How had Kavitha been feeling after the late calls?
qa.a: Kavitha felt weighed down and sleepless, carrying Tarun's distress as if it were Kavitha's own.

qa.q: How did Kavitha support Tarun while protecting sleep and energy?
qa.a: Kavitha listened fully at lunch, checked the guess about his feelings, suggested the confidential counselling line, and asked to keep chats to lunchtime.

qa.q: What was Tarun actually feeling about his manager?
qa.a: Tarun felt scared about losing his job, not humiliated as Kavitha had guessed.

grounding: Shows a young professional comforting a colleague without absorbing all his distress, checking empathic guesses and referring him to help.

passage: By the canal outside the village, Swati talked for almost an hour. Her grandmother had been bedridden since the monsoon, her parents were working in Ludhiana, and Swati was lifting, feeding and washing Dadi alone before and after teaching every day. Vijay listened, handing her the flask of tea. He felt the weight of it settle on his own chest; he wanted to promise he'd fix everything. Instead he checked. "You sound exhausted. Is it more tiredness, or more that you feel alone with it?" Swati wiped her face. "Alone. Tired too, but mostly alone." He nodded. "I can't carry this for you, and I'd do it badly. But the ASHA didi visits bedridden patients, and the women's group at the temple has a rota for helping families. Shall we go to the ASHA didi together tomorrow after school?" Swati let out a breath. "Yes. Together." Walking back, Vijay noticed his own shoulders felt lighter too.

qa.q: Where were Swati's parents working?
qa.a: In Ludhiana.

qa.q: What was Swati mainly feeling, according to her?
qa.a: Swati felt mostly alone with the caring, as well as tired.

qa.q: How did Vijay support Swati without taking on all her distress?
qa.a: He listened, checked his guess about her feelings, admitted he couldn't carry it for her, and offered to go with her to the ASHA didi and the women's group.

qa.q: How might Swati's grandmother benefit from Vijay's suggestion?
qa.a: Dadi could get regular visits from the ASHA didi and help from the women's group, so her care wouldn't depend on one exhausted granddaughter.

grounding: Shows a young adult listening with empathy, checking the guessed feeling, and pointing a friend to local help rather than absorbing it all.

passage: Vinita, you asked whether forgiving Radhika means you have to be friends again. Let me, Imran, tell you about Salim. At twenty-five we opened a small printing shop in Aligarh together. Twice I found he'd taken cash from the till. Twice he cried, swore it was the last time, and I believed him. The third time, I closed the partnership. People said, "He's your childhood friend, forgive him." And in the end I did forgive him, slowly, over years. I stopped wishing him harm. When his mother died, I went to the funeral. But I never went into business with him again, and I never lent him money again. Forgiving was for my own heart. Trust was a separate thing, and he had used up his chances. So forgive Radhika if you can, when you're ready. That doesn't mean you owe her your secrets again.

qa.q: Where did Imran and Salim open their shop?
qa.a: In Aligarh.

qa.q: How did Imran feel after the third time Salim took cash?
qa.a: Imran felt betrayed and finished with trusting him, closing the partnership despite pressure to forgive.

qa.q: What choice in the story separated forgiveness from trust?
qa.a: Imran forgave Salim slowly over years, even going to his mother's funeral, but never went into business with him or lent him money again.

qa.q: How might Salim have felt when Imran came to his mother's funeral?
qa.a: Salim may have felt surprised and touched, sensing Imran no longer wished him harm, even though the partnership was over.

grounding: An elder describes forgiving a partner who broke trust repeatedly while choosing not to renew the partnership.

passage: The wedding hall in Nagpur was loud with the band, and Uma had managed to avoid Seema through the haldi and the lunch. Two years ago they had shared a flat, until Seema started reading Uma's phone, locking her out when she came home late, and once throwing a steel glass at the wall beside her head. Uma had moved out overnight with her cousin's help. Now Seema caught her by the dessert counter, eyes wet. "Uma, I've changed. I'm in therapy. I'm so sorry. Can we be friends again?" Uma felt the old tightness in her chest. She kept her voice level. "I'm glad you're getting help. I accept your apology. But I'm not going to be in touch again." Seema's face crumpled. "Not even messages?" "No." Uma walked back to her cousin Neha's table and sat where she could see the door. "All okay?" Neha asked. "Yes. I said what I needed to."

qa.q: Who helped Uma move out?
qa.a: Her cousin.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when Seema caught her at the dessert counter?
qa.a: Uma felt the old tightness in her chest, wary and anxious, yet steady enough to speak clearly.

qa.q: How did Uma set her terms?
qa.a: She acknowledged Seema's apology and her getting help but clearly said she would not be in touch again, then returned to a safe spot beside her cousin.

qa.q: How did Seema react to Uma's answer?
qa.a: Seema's face crumpled; she seemed hurt and hoped for at least messages, but Uma held the boundary.

grounding: Shows a young adult accepting an apology but choosing not to renew contact with someone who was controlling and frightening, keeping herself safe.

passage: Reena turned up at Gurpreet's Chandigarh flat with a box of pinnis and an apology. "I'm sorry about the move. I promised to help, and I didn't come. Again." It was the third time in a year: the birthday dinner she'd skipped, the hospital visit she'd forgotten, and now Gurpreet carrying boxes up four floors alone. Gurpreet had been angry for a week. Now, looking at Reena's anxious face, she felt the anger soften but not disappear. "I forgive you," she said slowly. "I don't want to lose you as a friend. But I'm changing something. I'll still meet you for chai and films. For things I really need, like moves or hospital, I'll ask someone else. Not to punish you. So I don't get hurt again." Reena flinched, then nodded. "That's fair. I'd rather have chai with you than nothing." They opened the pinnis on the unpacked boxes.

qa.q: How many floors did Gurpreet carry boxes up alone?
qa.a: Four floors.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as Reena apologised?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt her week-long anger softening but not gone, torn between wanting the friendship and not wanting to be hurt again.

qa.q: What terms did Gurpreet set, and why are they sensible?
qa.a: She forgave Reena and kept the friendship for chai and films, but decided to ask others for things she truly needs, protecting herself without ending the bond.

qa.q: How did Reena respond to the new terms?
qa.a: Reena flinched but accepted them as fair, preferring a lighter friendship to none.

grounding: Shows a young adult forgiving a friend who repeatedly let her down while setting clear terms that protect her.

passage: Mahima, you apologised to the client eleven times in that email. I counted. Let me, Afreen, tell you what I learned the hard way. At twenty-five, working at a travel agency in Lucknow, I booked a family of six to Goa on the wrong date. When I noticed, I hid it for two days, hoping to fix it quietly. It got worse. When it came out, I swung the other way: I cried in my manager's cabin, called myself useless, and said sorry so many times she ended up comforting me instead of fixing anything. The family still had no tickets. The next time I made a mistake, a wrong hotel booking, I went to her within the hour. "I booked the wrong hotel for the Mehras. That's my error. I've already called the right hotel; they have rooms. I'll confirm with the family by four." She said, "Thank you. Good." That's all it needed. One sorry, the facts, the fix.

qa.q: How many people were in the family booked on the wrong date?
qa.a: Six; it was a family of six.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when hiding the mistake for two days?
qa.a: Afreen felt afraid and anxious, hoping to fix it quietly rather than admit it.

qa.q: What choice the second time made the difference?
qa.a: Owning the wrong hotel booking within the hour, stating the error, the fix already under way and when the family would hear, with one brief sorry.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt when Afreen cried and called herself useless?
qa.a: The manager likely felt pulled into comforting Afreen instead of solving the problem, while the family still had no tickets.

grounding: An elder recalls hiding an error and then over-apologising, and learning that a brief, factual acknowledgement with a fix works best.

passage: Twelve minutes before the board meeting, Harish noticed it: the revenue figure on slide three was last year's, not this year's. His slide. His mistake. The board members were already taking their seats in the glass room at the Bengaluru office. His first instinct was to blame the template, which was old. His second was to spiral into apology. He did neither. He walked straight to Leela, the finance director, who was checking her notes by the door. "Leela, quickly: the revenue on slide three is last year's figure. That's my error. The correct one is 48 crore. I can fix the slide in five minutes, or you can say it aloud if we run out of time." Leela glanced at her watch. "Fix it. Send it to me by 10:55." At 10:53 the corrected slide was in her inbox. Afterwards she said only, "Thanks for catching it before they did."

qa.q: What was wrong with slide three?
qa.a: The revenue figure was last year's, not this year's.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he noticed the error?
qa.a: Harish felt a jolt of panic, tempted first to blame the old template and then to spiral into apology.

qa.q: What made Harish's approach to the error effective?
qa.a: He owned it quickly and briefly, gave the correct figure and two fix options, avoiding both defensiveness and over-apology.

qa.q: How did Leela seem to feel about how Harish handled it?
qa.a: Leela seemed calm and appreciative, thanking him for catching it before the board did.

grounding: Shows a young professional under time pressure owning an error early, explaining the fix, and avoiding both defensiveness and over-apology.

passage: "Sarita, the vendor got the old price list," Siddharth said, leaning over her desk at the Pune office. "They've quoted on the wrong rates." Sarita's face went hot. Her first words were already forming: "You sent me the wrong file." She'd heard people do that: blame the file, the system, the other person. She stopped herself and opened her sent folder. There it was: the old list, attached by her, on Tuesday. "You're right. I attached the old list. My mistake." Siddharth blinked, clearly expecting an argument. "Okay. What now?" "I'll email them the correct list now, say it was my error, and ask them to re-quote by Friday. I'll copy you." She did it in ten minutes. No speech, no drama. Later Siddharth said, "Honestly, that was refreshing. The last person I flagged something to argued for an hour."

qa.q: When did Sarita attach the old list?
qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when Siddharth pointed out the error?
qa.a: Sarita felt embarrassed and defensive, face hot, tempted to blame Siddharth's file.

qa.q: How did Sarita handle the error?
qa.a: She checked the facts, owned the mistake briefly, and explained the fix: sending the correct list, naming it as her error and asking for a re-quote by Friday.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel about Sarita's response?
qa.a: Siddharth found it refreshing, having expected an argument like the last person he'd flagged something to.

grounding: Shows a young professional resisting defensiveness, owning an error briefly and factually, and fixing it.

passage: When Gurpreet came to stay at Binita's flat in Guwahati, Binita cooked her best fish curry and rice. "More rice?" she asked, once. "No, no, I'm fine," Gurpreet said, the way she always did. Binita nodded and put the pot away. Gurpreet went to bed hungry and ate a packet of biscuits at midnight. The next day at lunch the same thing happened. This time Binita noticed Gurpreet eyeing the pot. "You said no yesterday too," she said slowly. "Did you mean no?" Gurpreet laughed, embarrassed. "At home in Ludhiana, you never say yes the first time. The host asks three times and then piles it on your plate anyway." Binita laughed too. "In my house, if you say no, we believe you!" After that Binita offered twice, watched the plate, and once just served a spoonful without asking. Gurpreet ate it gratefully.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet eat at midnight?
qa.a: A packet of biscuits.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when Binita put the pot away?
qa.a: Gurpreet was probably a bit dismayed and awkward, still hungry but held back by the habit of refusing the first offer.

qa.q: What did Binita learn to do as a host?

"Urmila Nani, let me carry that bag."
"No, no, beta, I can manage." Nani shifted the cloth bag to her other hand on the stairs of Pooja's building in Indore.
Pooja watched her stop on the landing, breathing hard. "Nani. Give it. Please."
"Arre, you young people think we're made of glass." But her fingers loosened, and Pooja took the bag.
Inside, Pooja asked, "Tea? Or do you want to lie down first?"
"Nothing, nothing. Don't trouble yourself."
Pooja had heard that "nothing" her whole life. She put the kettle on anyway and set a pillow on the divan. "The tea's already on. And the pillow's there if you want it. No trouble."
Nani sat down, looked at the pillow, and after a moment tucked her feet up. "Only for five minutes."
"Only five."
When Pooja came back with the tea, Nani was asleep, glasses still on. Pooja slid them off gently and let the tea go cold.

qa.a: She was probably tired and a little proud, breathing hard but not wanting to seem weak or be a trouble.

qa.a: She offered again, read cues like the hard breathing, and quietly prepared tea and a pillow so Nani could accept without having to ask.

qa.a: Nani might have sat up exhausted, too polite to rest, instead of getting the sleep she clearly needed.

I realised that here, if I needed something, I'd have to say it plainly, even if it felt rude. It took practice: "Yes, please, I'd love more." I hope you're well. I'd like to ask for a small change that would help me do my job better.

In large meetings and video calls I sometimes miss parts of the discussion, especially when several people talk at once or someone's microphone is poor. I've been getting by by asking colleagues afterwards, but I'm worried I'm missing things that matter.
Could we switch on live captions for team video calls, and could I have the seat on the right side of the table, near whoever is presenting? If captions aren't possible for every call, a short written summary of decisions after the big meetings would also work well.
I'm happy to talk about it whenever suits you.
Thanks very much,
Noor

passage:
Friday night
Had to talk to Mahima today about being late. Fourth time this month, and the breakfast rush fell apart again because the coffee station wasn't ready.
I remember how my old supervisor at the bakery used to do it: sarcasm in front of everyone. "Oh, look who decided to join us, the princess." I used to cry in the storeroom. I swore I'd never do that.
So I took Mahima to the back at the end of the shift, just us, and kept my voice low. "You've come in after eight four times this month. When the coffee station isn't set up, the whole line waits and customers walk out. I need you here by 7:45. Is something making mornings hard?" She went quiet, then said the bus route had changed. We worked out an earlier bus, and she'll message me by seven if she's stuck.
She thanked me. I didn't enjoy it, but I didn't feel like a bully either.
Noor
